dedupe_keys.name: orange county groundwater replenishment system california global potable reuse case study 1 unsw and awrcoe

description: This case study is the first in a global series on potable reuse, written by the University of New South Wales for the Australian Water Recycling Centre of Excellence, and it covers the Orange County Groundwater Replenishment System in California. It traces the scheme from the 1965 start of secondary treatment and the Water Factory 21 pilots, which used reverse osmosis from 1977 to supply a seawater intrusion barrier, to the 2008 GWRS, the largest advanced water purification facility of its kind, built after drivers of drought, seawater intrusion, population growth and transport cost. The plant makes 70 million gallons of purified water a day for injection and recharge for about 600,000 residents, at an estimated design and barrier and pipeline cost of 481 million dollars. Its permit is approved by the state health department and the regional water board, and more than 500 parameters are monitored, with tables of water quality for 2008 to 2012 comparing secondary effluent and final product water with permit limits. Coverage: one scheme, with figures to 2012. Access: free PDF; licence not stated. Caveats: dates from 2014 and is a descriptive report, not a dataset. It informs simulation of advanced treatment trains, aquifer recharge and drought supply planning, and lists no linked catalogue records.
